title: Why Metallic Paint Can't Be Pre-Mixed (It's Physics)
description: Ever wondered why metallic/aluminum paint gets mixed fresh right before use instead of coming pre-mixed? There's a real physics reason behind it. AI-narrated commentary exploring the everyday science of 'leafing' paint.

hook_candidates.text: Why does metallic paint have to be mixed right before you use it, and never before?
Leave metallic paint mixed too long and it silently stops looking metallic at all.
You'd think paint gets mixed once at the factory and stays that way — metallic paint breaks that rule completely.

beats.text: Why does metallic paint have to be mixed right before you use it, and never before?
beats.broll_query: opening metallic paint can lid closeup

beats.text: It's really two ingredients kept apart: aluminum powder, and the varnish it floats in.
Mix them and let it sit, and those flakes just sink and clump at the bottom.
beats.broll_query: metal particles settling in liquid slow motion

beats.text: Mixed fresh, they drift upward and align flat at the surface — chemists call it 'leafing.'
beats.broll_query: shiny metallic paint surface close up

beats.text: That thin aligned layer is what gives the paint its mirror-like metallic shine.
Wait too long, and that alignment collapses into a dull, uneven finish.
So 'mix immediately before use' isn't a suggestion — it's a countdown on real chemistry.
